stories.headline: WHO declares Central Africa Ebola outbreak an international public health emergency
stories.summary: The WHO has declared the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda a Public Health Emergency of International Concern, citing rising confirmed and suspected cases, cross-border spread, healthcare worker deaths, and uncertainty about the true scale of transmission. The agency is not recommending travel restrictions, but is urging surveillance, contact tracing, emergency response, and trusted community engagement.
stories.pastoral_note: This is a moment to pray for mercy and wisdom, especially for local churches and health workers who often become trusted messengers in crisis. Fear spreads quickly; so can embodied neighbour-love.

stories.headline: Open Doors calls churches to pray for persecuted Christians after Pentecost
stories.summary: Open Doors is inviting churches across Africa to mark Persecution Sunday on May 31, framing prayer for the persecuted church around Matthew 22:39, Romans 12:9-21, and John 13:35. The movement emphasizes standing with believers who cannot gather freely, encouraging one another, and asking God to renew the church in costly neighbour-love.
stories.pastoral_note: The timing is powerful: right after Pentecost, the Spirit-filled church in Acts quickly becomes a suffering church. This could serve as a reminder that charismatic power and costly witness belong together.

stories.headline: Talk of a religious ‘vibe shift’ highlights renewed openness among younger adults
stories.summary: Christian Standard reports that signs of renewed spiritual openness are emerging alongside long-term secularization: Pew data suggests Christian identification has stabilized in recent years, while Barna/Gloo point to increased Bible reading and frequent churchgoing among Gen Z churchgoers. The picture remains mixed, but the cultural mood may be more open to faith conversations than many pastors assume.
stories.pastoral_note: This is not a reason for triumphalism, but it is a reason to keep doors wide open. People may be less hostile to Jesus than they are wary of institutions; patient invitation matters.

stories.headline: Tech companies seek faith leaders’ help in shaping ethical AI
stories.summary: AP reports that representatives from companies including Anthropic and OpenAI met with faith leaders in New York for an inaugural Faith-AI Covenant roundtable. Organizers hope to develop moral norms for AI across religious traditions, while critics note the difficulty of defining ‘moral AI’ and the risk of outsourcing ethics to branding exercises.
stories.pastoral_note: This is a discipleship issue, not just a tech issue. The church should neither fearfully retreat nor naively bless the tools; we can ask what forms love, truthfulness, humility, and human dignity in an AI-saturated world.

stories.headline: HBR asks whether leaders should treat AI like a teammate
stories.summary: Harvard Business Review’s leadership page highlights ‘Should You Treat AI Like a Teammate?’, a May 12 Insider piece gathering current HBR thinking on AI agents, coworkers, automation, motivation, and management. The framing reflects a fast-shifting leadership question: how to integrate powerful tools without confusing assistance with agency, accountability, or trust.
stories.pastoral_note: For church teams, the leadership lesson is clarity. Tools can help with work; they cannot carry calling, character, prayer, or pastoral responsibility.

stories.headline: Fraser Valley market shows early stabilization while buyers retain strong selection
stories.summary: The Fraser Valley Real Estate Board’s April 2026 report says benchmark prices edged upward for the second consecutive month, sales rose month-over-month and year-over-year, and sellers continued to enter the market. Elevated inventory is keeping conditions favourable for buyers, with the market described as active but balanced.
stories.pastoral_note: Housing remains one of the region’s quiet discipleship pressures. Stabilization may help some families breathe, but affordability anxiety is still a pastoral reality in the Fraser Valley.

stories.headline: New schools in eastern DR Congo offer children hope amid war and displacement
stories.summary: UN News reports that a new two-year, $10 million Education Cannot Wait programme will support more than 62,000 crisis-affected children in Ituri Province, prioritizing girls, displaced children, and vulnerable students. In a region where 5.3 million people are internally displaced and millions of children are out of school, classrooms are being described as protection, stabilization, and a place where dreams of peace can grow.
stories.pastoral_note: Even in places marked by violence, small acts of faithful rebuilding matter. A classroom can become a signpost of the kingdom: children protected, futures imagined, peace practiced.

stories.headline: Gen Z may be asking a different question about evil: why don’t bad things happen to bad people?
stories.summary: Christianity Today reflects on a shift in Gen Z’s theodicy questions. Rather than primarily asking why good people suffer, many students are asking why oppressors are not judged and why victims are not vindicated. The article notes that some students find biblical mercy harder to accept than biblical judgment, especially against the backdrop of abuse scandals and public injustice.
stories.pastoral_note: This creates an evangelistic opening: the gospel does not minimize justice, but it also reveals a Judge who bears judgment in mercy. Preaching grace today must name victims, confront evil, and still proclaim forgiveness without making it cheap.
